research_brief.research_summary: The textbook answer (Rayleigh scattering: air molecules scatter short wavelengths far more than long ones, roughly 1/wavelength^4) is well covered, but most short explainers stop there and leave the obvious follow-up unanswered: if shorter waves scatter more, why isn't the sky violet? The answer (less violet in sunlight plus eyes far more sensitive to blue) is the underserved 'aha', and red sunsets are the same physics seen from the other side.

data_points.claim: Rayleigh scattering intensity is inversely proportional to the fourth power of wavelength
Blue light (~425 nm) is scattered about 5.5x more than red light (~650 nm); the exact ratio depends on wavelengths chosen
Violet scatters even more than blue; the sky looks blue because sunlight contains less violet, some is absorbed high up, and human eyes are much less sensitive to violet
Clouds are white because droplets 100-1000x the wavelength scatter all colors about equally (Mie scattering)
At sunrise/sunset light crosses far more atmosphere, so blue is scattered out of the beam, leaving reds and oranges
The Moon has no air, so its daytime sky is black; Mars' thin dusty air gives a butterscotch sky and blue sunsets

misconceptions.myth: The sky is blue because it reflects the ocean
misconceptions.reality: Air scatters blue light; the sky is blue far inland too. (The ocean is mostly blue because water absorbs red.)

misconceptions.myth: Shorter waves scatter more, so the sky must be the shortest color we can see
misconceptions.reality: Violet scatters most, but sunlight has less of it and our eyes favor blue
